title: At the café
goal: Order drinks and snacks politely, use je voudrais, and meet the partitive articles du / de la.
bekal: use *du*, *de la*, *de l'* for things you can't count
ask for the check and pay: *l'addition, s'il vous plaît*
wave: Go back to **Unit 2** first: cover the French, then introduce Thomas to a friend from memory — say what he does and how long he has lived in Lyon.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — À la terrasse
dialogs.intro: Budi and Camille sit down on a café terrace. The waiter comes over.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Bonjour. Un café, s'il vous plaît.
lines.literal: good-day. a coffee, if-it to-you pleases.

lines.speaker: Serveur:
lines.text: Très bien. Et pour vous, monsieur ?
lines.id: Very good. And for you, sir?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Je voudrais un thé au lait, s'il vous plaît.

notes: **Je voudrais is the magic phrase.** Literally "I would want" — the polite form of *je veux* (I want). *Je veux un café* sounds like a small child's demand; *je voudrais un café* sounds like an adult. Always use this form in shops, restaurants and at counters.

**Un café means an espresso.** If you want a big milky coffee, order *un café au lait* or *un crème*. *Un café américain* is for a long, American-style coffee. Ordering plain "coffee" in France gets you a tiny cup gone in two sips.
**S'il vous plaît is not decoration.** Leaving it out in France isn't just a little impolite — it sounds rude. The full meaning is "if it pleases you". With friends: *s'il te plaît*.
**Vous désirez ?** is how waiters ask. Its relatives are *Vous prenez quelque chose ?* and *Qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?* You don't need to say them — just recognize them when you hear them.
**Ce sera tout ?** uses a future form you haven't learned yet, and there's no need to take it apart now. Just recognize it as "anything else?" and answer *c'est tout* (that's all) or *non, aussi…*

**The negative drops the article.** *Je bois du café* → *je ne bois pas **de** café*. This is not a minor exception but a major rule: after a negative, *du*, *de la*, *des*, *un*, *une* all shrink to **de**. Only *le, la, les* survive.
**Je t'invite** is literally "I invite you", and it's how French people say "I'm paying". The polite comeback: *non, c'est moi !* or *on partage* (let's split it).

grammars.title: Du, de la, de l' — articles for things you can't count
body: English can say "I drink coffee" with nothing in front of the noun. French can't: it has to mark that you're drinking *some* coffee, not all the coffee in the world — a bit like English "some", except that in French it's compulsory.
after: Three articles, three different meanings for what in English could all be "coffee": *j'aime **le** café* (I like coffee, in general), *je bois **du** café* (I drink coffee, some of it), *je voudrais **un** café* (I'd like a cup of coffee).
After *aimer*, *adorer*, *détester* it's always **le / la / les** — because what you like is the thing as a whole. This comes back in full in Unit 15.
⚠️ Leaving out the article entirely (*je bois café*) is the mistake that marks a foreign speaker fastest. Pick one, but never leave it empty.

grammars.title: Prendre and boire
body: Two verbs you can't avoid at a café. Both are irregular, and both double a consonant in the *ils* form.
after: *Prendre* covers far more than "to take": ordering food (*je prends une salade*), taking transport (*je prends le bus*), and taking medicine (*je prends un médicament*).
*Mangeons* slips in a silent **e** so the g stays soft. Other verbs ending in -ger do the same: *nous voyageons*, *nous changeons*.

blocks.text: What people really order in a French café. Learn them with their articles, as usual.

blocks.title: Lifesaver phrases
items: *Une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît.* — A table for two, please.
*Qu'est-ce que vous avez comme dessert ?* — What do you have for dessert?
*L'addition, s'il vous plaît.* — The check, please. In France the check never comes by itself; you have to ask for it.
*Je peux payer par carte ?* — Can I pay by card?
